The reasons behind each stop live in notebooks and memory.
Efficiency is debated instead of known.

architecture.title: Under the hood
architecture.intro: Six pieces, one flow of data. Select a piece to see what it does.

layers.name: PLC
layers.detail: Each machine’s controller already knows whether it is running, stopped or slow, and counts every part it makes. The MES reads those signals; it does not change how the machine is programmed.

layers.name: Collector
layers.detail: Picks up the PLC tags and publishes them with a timestamp, without extra wiring on the machines.

layers.name: Time-series store
layers.detail: Records every signal as it happens. It is the raw memory of the plant: what value each tag had, and when.

layers.name: Data pipeline
layers.detail: Brings new signals into the MES, translates each tag to its machine and hands the data to the database to interpret. Mapping a new tag is a configuration row, not new code.

layers.name: MES database
layers.detail: Where signals become facts: machine timelines, stop events, part counts, orders, shifts and OEE by machine, line and plant. All business rules live here, in one place.

layers.name: Screens
layers.detail: Operators see their line, start and pause orders, and add the reason for every stop. Managers see OEE by hour, shift and order.

flow.rule: Machines report facts. People explain them. Nobody can turn a breakdown into a “slow run”.

demo.disclaimer: Simulated data, not connected to a PLC

fault.prompt: You are the operator. Why did Machine 2 stop?

messages.idle: The line is running. Cause a breakdown to see what the MES does with it.
messages.unknown: The PLC reported the stop. The MES logged it as Unknown and counts it as unplanned until a person explains it.
messages.restart: Reason recorded. Restart the line to resume production.
messages.restarted: Line restarted. The stop stays in the log with its reason and its effect on OEE.

kpi.title: OEE: one number for real performance
kpi.intro: Overall Equipment Effectiveness multiplies three questions. 100% means only good parts, at full speed, with no unplanned stops.

factors.name: Availability
factors.question: Was it running when it should?
factors.loss: Lost to unplanned stops: breakdowns, missing material, lost signal.

factors.name: Performance
factors.question: Did it run at ideal speed?
factors.loss: Lost to slow running and short micro-stops.

example.body: An illustrative 8-hour shift: 90% availability × 85% performance × 97% quality. Of 480 minutes paid for, only 356 produced good parts at full speed. The other 124 minutes are the opportunity, and the MES shows where they went.

phases.name: Before the shift
items: Routes set product, line and ideal speed
Orders load from an Excel template

phases.name: During the shift
items: The operator starts an order on a line
The MES counts parts and detects stops
The operator adds each stop’s reason

phases.name: After the shift
items: Reasons can be corrected until end of day
The shift is then closed and locked

rollup.title: From one machine to the whole plant
rollup.body: Results roll up the way a plant really works. A line is paced by its slowest machine, not by a simple average, so the same loss is never counted twice.

levels.name: Machine
levels.body: Where every result starts: stops, speed and counts.

levels.name: Line
levels.body: Availability from its last machine, speed from its bottleneck.

levels.name: Plant
levels.body: All lines combined, weighted by their time.
